newsitem.title: UK: SBC Warburg cuts 1997-99 gold price forecasts.
newsitem.headline: SBC Warburg cuts 1997-99 gold price forecasts.

text.p: SBC Warburg, a division of Swiss Bank Corporation, has cut its 1997 average gold price forecast by 3.6 percent to $345 per ounce from $352.

The 1998 and 1999 forecasts have been trimmed by 9.5 percent and 13 percent respectively to $335 for both years from $370 and $385, according to SBC Warburg's global head of commodity research Peter Richardson.
"This is a conservative outlook. We are basically saying to investors, 'be very cautious'," Richardson said.

He said the apparently optimistic forecast for this year's price reflected so-far solid support at $337.00 and physical demand for metal limiting the downside pressures. Gold fixed in London on Thursday morning at $337.90.

But referring to the medium term outlook, the SBC Warburg report stated, "This extended period of low prices is designed to reflect our concerns about a number of key issues that are expected to dominate the gold market over the next two and a half years."
Key factors involved were the absence of investment buying anticipated in a future of moderate sustainable growth and low inflation.
There was also the continuing threat of official sales and lending from central banks and other institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
But also significant was continued forward selling by producers and the likelihood that mine supply would be cut only marginally at the forecast price levels.
An estimated 753 tonnes of additional gold would be delivered to the market through hedging by new and existing mines protecting themselves against low prices during the period.

The increase was likely due to new management and ownership in the South African industry possibly triggering new or increased hedging programmes, fresh hedging from North American producers which had unwound earlier positions and new mines being obliged to hedge by the terms of their project financing agreements.
"Investors can't look for salvation from the supply and demand fundamentals in gold mining as they can in other industries," said Richardson.
He estimated that at the report's forecast prices, only a net 32 tonnes of mine production would be cut due to unprofitability in 1999.
"Obviously if the price turns out to be lower, then there will be larger losses of production," Richardson said.
However the estimated mine cutback would be more than offset by higher sales from central banks.
SBC Warburg estimated net official sales at 250 tonnes this year, 263 tonnes in 1998 and 276 tonnes in 1999.
There was an increased chance that the IMF would sell around five million ounces of gold to raise funds for its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility to aid the world's poorest countries.
Even if this did not happen until the next century, the perception that it was forthcoming would depress the market, Richardson said.

Changing attitudes in the central banking community most vividly witnessed by recent announcements about revaluing gold reserves from Germany and Switzerland would "create a much more fluid environment" in which IMF policy on gold reserves would be discussed, Richardson said.
